title: Mutable default argument
prompt: add_tag() should return a fresh tag list for each post unless one is passed in. Why do tags from one post show up on another?
answer: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call without `tags` shares the same list. `second` comes back as ["python", "sql"], and the list keeps growing for the life of the process.
fix:
def add_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags
followUp: Interviewers often ask why `None` is the conventional sentinel and whether the same trap applies to dicts and sets (it does).
code:
def add_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] = []) -> list[str]:
    """Append a tag and return the list of tags."""
    if tag not in tags:
        tags.append(tag)
    return tags


first = add_tag("python")   # ["python"]
second = add_tag("sql")     # expected ["sql"]

title: f-string SQL query
prompt: This looks up a user by email for the login form. What's the problem?
answer: The email is pasted into the SQL text, so input like `' OR '1'='1` changes the query and returns the first user, letting an attacker log in as someone else. Let the driver bind the value instead.
fix: cur.execute("SELECT id, email, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,))
followUp: Expect a follow-up on why escaping quotes by hand is not enough, and how ORMs parameterize queries for you.

title: Check-then-create directory
prompt: Several worker processes call ensure_dir() at startup. Occasionally one crashes with FileExistsError. Why?
answer: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race. Two processes can both see that the path doesn't exist, then both call makedirs, and the slower one raises FileExistsError. Make the operation itself idempotent instead of checking first.
fix: os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True)
followUp: A good answer generalizes: prefer atomic operations (exist_ok, O_EXCL, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT) over check-then-act.

title: Last N items with a slice
prompt: last_n() powers the "recent activity" widget. A user set their widget size to 0. What do they see?
answer: When n is 0, `-n` is also 0, and `items[0:]` is the whole list. Asking for zero items returns everything.
fix: return items[max(len(items) - n, 0):]
followUp: Interviewers like this one because the code is correct for every n except the boundary. Ask yourself about 0, 1, and n > len(items).

title: Logging every request header
prompt: This middleware was added to debug a production issue. What should a reviewer flag?
answer: Request headers include `Authorization` bearer tokens, session cookies and API keys. Writing them to logs leaks live credentials to everyone with log access and to every log pipeline they pass through.
followUp: Mention that leaked tokens must be rotated, not just deleted from logs.
code:
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def log_request(request) -> None:
    logger.info("%s %s", request.method, request.path)
    logger.info("headers: %s", dict(request.headers))

title: Getting the last element
prompt: latestMessage() should return the newest message in the chat. Why is the preview always empty?
answer: Arrays are zero-indexed, so the last element is at `length - 1`. `messages[messages.length]` is undefined, and reading `.text` on it throws a TypeError.
fix: const last = messages[messages.length - 1]; // or messages.at(-1)
followUp: Bonus points for mentioning Array.prototype.at(-1).

title: Falsy zero in a stock label
prompt: formatStock() renders the stock badge on product cards. What does a sold-out product show?
answer: `!count` is true for 0 as well as for null and undefined, so a sold-out product shows "Stock unknown" instead of being treated as zero stock.
fix:
if (count == null) return "Stock unknown";
  if (count === 0) return "Sold out";
followUp: Know the falsy values cold: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN.

title: Scroll listener per page view
prompt: trackScrollDepth() runs on every client-side route change in a single-page app. What goes wrong after a few minutes of browsing?
answer: A new scroll listener is added on every navigation and never removed. Old listeners keep running (and keep their closures alive), so each scroll does more and more work and memory grows for the whole session.
followUp: Removing a listener requires the same function reference that was added, so name the handler.

title: Sorting numbers with sort()
prompt: topScores() should return the three highest scores. What does it return for [100, 25, 9, 1000]?
answer: Without a comparator, sort() converts values to strings and sorts them lexicographically: [100, 1000, 25, 9]. Reversed, that gives [9, 25, 1000], and 100 is dropped.
fix: return [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a).slice(0, 3);
followUp: Mention that copying first ([...scores]) matters because sort() mutates in place, or use toSorted().

title: Secret key in front-end code
prompt: This runs in the browser when the user clicks "Pay". What's the problem?
answer: Everything shipped to the browser is public. Anyone can read the live secret key from the bundle or the network tab and use it to issue refunds, read customers, or create charges. Secret keys belong on the server; the browser should call your own endpoint.
followUp: Distinguish publishable keys (safe in the browser) from secret keys (never).

title: Rendering comments with innerHTML
prompt: renderComment() displays user comments under a post. What can an attacker do?
answer: User text is parsed as HTML. A comment like `` runs script in every reader's browser (stored XSS), which can steal sessions or act as the user.
followUp: Mention textContent, framework auto-escaping, and sanitizers like DOMPurify when HTML is truly required.

title: Search-as-you-type results
prompt: onQueryChange() runs on every keystroke. Users sometimes see results for "re" after typing "react". Why?
answer: Requests can finish out of order. If the slow response for "re" arrives after the fast one for "react", it overwrites the newer results. Only the latest request should be allowed to update the UI.
followUp: An AbortController that cancels the previous request is an equally good answer, and you can mention debouncing.

title: Reading preferences from localStorage
prompt: loadTheme() runs on page load. It works for returning visitors. What happens on someone's first visit?
answer: On a first visit getItem returns null. The `!` hides that from TypeScript, `JSON.parse(null)` returns null, and `prefs.theme` throws a TypeError that breaks page load.
followUp: Also consider corrupted JSON: wrap JSON.parse in try/catch for data you don't control.

title: Pending tasks filter
prompt: The "To do" tab shows the result of pendingTasks(). Users say it lists the tasks they already finished. Find the bug.
answer: filter keeps the items for which the callback returns true, so this keeps the completed tasks. Pending tasks are the ones where done is false.
fix: return tasks.filter((task) => !task.done);
followUp: A quick unit test with one done and one pending task catches this instantly; say so.

title: Awaiting requests one by one
prompt: loadAvatars() fetches 50 independent user profiles for a team page. It takes ~10 seconds. Why?
answer: Each request waits for the previous one to finish, so total time is the sum of all latencies (50 × ~200ms). The requests are independent and can run concurrently.
followUp: Strong candidates add that very large lists need a concurrency limit, or a batch endpoint.

title: Counting words in goroutines
prompt: CountWords splits work across goroutines. Under load the process dies with "fatal error: concurrent map writes". Why?
answer: Go maps are not safe for concurrent writes. Several goroutines update `counts` at once, which the runtime detects and treats as a fatal error that can't be recovered.
followUp: Better still: count into a local map per goroutine and merge at the end, so the lock is taken once per document.

title: Average of an empty slice
prompt: Average() is used on the latency dashboard. What happens for a service with no requests yet?
answer: With an empty slice, len is 0 and integer division by zero panics at runtime ("integer divide by zero"), crashing the dashboard handler.
followUp: Mention whether 0 is the right answer for "no data", or whether returning (int, bool) is clearer.

title: Unclosed HTTP response body
prompt: FetchStatus() is called every few seconds by a health checker. After a day the service runs out of file descriptors. Why?
answer: The response body is never closed. Each call leaves a connection and its file descriptor open, and they can't be returned to the pool, so the process eventually hits its open-file limit.
followUp: Some interviewers also ask about draining the body (io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)) so keep-alive connections can be reused.

title: Hard-coded JWT signing key
prompt: This signs session tokens for the API. What should block this PR?
answer: The signing key is in source control. Anyone who can read the repo (or a leaked copy) can mint valid tokens for any user, including admins. Load it from a secret store or environment at startup, and fail if it's missing.
followUp: Mention key rotation and that a guessable HS256 secret can be brute-forced offline from any issued token.

title: Upload file-type check
prompt: validateUpload() should only accept PNG files. What does it actually allow?
answer: The condition is inverted: every file that is not a PNG passes validation, and real PNGs are rejected.
followUp: Also point out that extensions are user-controlled; check the file's magic bytes (http.DetectContentType) for real validation.

title: Summing an array
prompt: total() adds up a cart's line items. Why does it throw on every call?
answer: Valid indexes run from 0 to length - 1. With `<=` the loop reads index `length` on its last pass and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
fix: for (int i = 0; i < lineItemsCents.length; i++) {
followUp: An enhanced for loop (for (long c : lineItemsCents)) removes the index, and the bug, entirely.

title: Calling Optional.get()
prompt: greetingFor() builds the email greeting for the password-reset flow. What happens for an email that isn't registered?
answer: findByEmail returns Optional.empty() for unknown emails, and get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException. The reset endpoint returns a 500, which also tells attackers which emails exist.
followUp: Optional exists to force you to handle absence; get() without isPresent() defeats the point.

title: JDBC connection never closed
prompt: emailExists() is called on every signup. After some traffic, all requests hang waiting for a database connection. Why?
answer: The connection, statement and result set are never closed, so every call keeps a pooled connection checked out. Once the pool is exhausted, new requests block until they time out.
followUp: Explain why try-with-resources beats a finally block: it closes in reverse order and keeps suppressed exceptions.

title: Comparing strings with ==
prompt: isAdmin() gates the admin dashboard. Why are real admins being locked out?
answer: `==` compares object references, not contents. The header value is a new String built at runtime, so it is never the same object as the "admin" literal and the check is always false.
fix: return "admin".equals(role);
followUp: Putting the literal first also avoids a NullPointerException when the header is missing. (And never trust a client-supplied role header for authorization in real code.)

title: Building a CSV with +=
prompt: toCsv() exports 200k rows. It takes minutes and churns the garbage collector. Why?
answer: Strings are immutable, so each += copies everything built so far into a new string. Over n rows that is O(n²) copying and a huge amount of garbage.
followUp: Mention that the compiler's StringBuilder optimization applies within a single expression, not across loop iterations.

title: January revenue with BETWEEN
prompt: This should total all orders placed in January. Finance says the number is too low. Why? (created_at is a TIMESTAMP.)
answer: '2025-01-31' means midnight at the start of Jan 31, and BETWEEN is inclusive of exactly that instant. Every order placed later on Jan 31 is excluded.
fix:
WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2025-02-01';
followUp: Half-open ranges (>= start, < next start) work for every precision and avoid end-of-month arithmetic.

title: Dynamic SQL in a stored function
prompt: This PL/pgSQL function backs an admin search box. What's the vulnerability?
answer: The parameter is concatenated into a dynamically executed string, so a name containing a quote can rewrite the query. Code inside the database is just as injectable as application code.
followUp: Here the query doesn't need to be dynamic at all; a plain RETURN QUERY SELECT with the parameter is simplest.

title: Filtering with = NULL
prompt: This should list users who haven't verified their email (verified_at is NULL). Why does it always return zero rows?
answer: Any comparison with NULL using = yields NULL (unknown), never TRUE, so no row passes the filter. NULL checks need IS NULL.
fix: WHERE verified_at IS NULL
followUp: Related traps: NOT IN with a NULL in the list, and COUNT(column) skipping NULLs.
code:
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE verified_at = NULL
ORDER BY created_at;

title: Leaderboard top 10
prompt: This query feeds the "Top 10 players" leaderboard. Why is the leaderboard full of beginners?
answer: ASC sorts from lowest to highest, so LIMIT 10 keeps the ten worst scores. A top-N query needs descending order.
fix: ORDER BY best_score DESC
followUp: Also discuss ties: should players with equal scores share a rank (RANK() vs ROW_NUMBER())?
code:
SELECT player_id, MAX(score) AS best_score
FROM game_results
GROUP BY player_id
ORDER BY best_score ASC
LIMIT 10;

title: Leading-wildcard LIKE
prompt: users has 30M rows and a B-tree index on email. This query takes 20 seconds. Why?
answer: A B-tree index is ordered by the start of the value, so a pattern that starts with % can't use it. The database scans all 30M rows.
followUp: Alternatives worth naming: an index on reverse(email), or a trigram (pg_trgm) index for general substring search.
